questions.stem: The total number of bones in an adult human skeleton is:

options.option_text: 300 bones, present in newborn infants
206 bones, the standard adult count
300 bones, the standard adult count
180 bones, the count after fusion in old age

questions.explanation: Adult — 206 bones. Newborn — ~270-300 bones, many of which fuse during growth (e.g., the cranial sutures, the sacrum's 5 fused vertebrae, coccyx fusion). Adult skeleton: AXIAL (skull, vertebral column, ribs, sternum) = 80 bones; APPENDICULAR (limbs + girdles) = 126 bones. Largest bone: femur (~26% of adult height). Smallest: stapes (in the middle ear). Distractors 1 and 3 confuse newborn with adult counts. Distractor 4 — adult count does not drop further after maturity.

questions.stem: The longest and strongest bone in the human body is the:

options.option_text: Tibia, the larger of the two leg-bones below the knee
Femur, the thigh bone running from hip to knee
Humerus, the single bone of the upper arm
Sternum, the long flat bone in the centre of the chest

questions.explanation: Femur (thigh bone) — the longest, heaviest, and strongest bone in the human body; ~26% of adult height. Bears body weight when standing or walking. Distractor 1 = tibia (shin bone), 2nd longest. Distractor 3 = humerus, upper-arm bone. Distractor 4 = sternum (breastbone), flat not long. Smallest bone — STAPES (3 mm) in the middle ear.

questions.stem: The joint between the upper and lower leg at the knee is best classified as a:

options.option_text: Ball-and-socket joint, like the hip or shoulder
Hinge joint, allowing only forward-back movement
Pivot joint, allowing rotational movement only
Saddle joint, found at the base of the thumb

questions.explanation: Knee — hinge joint (allows flexion + extension only, like a door hinge). Other hinge joints — elbow, ankle, finger interphalangeal joints. BALL-AND-SOCKET (hip, shoulder) — three-axis movement. PIVOT (atlas-axis at neck, allowing 'no' head-shake) — rotation around one axis. SADDLE (base of thumb / carpometacarpal joint) — opposable-thumb saddle motion. GLIDING (between vertebrae, between wrist bones) — small sliding movements.

questions.stem: Skeletal (voluntary) muscles, smooth (involuntary) muscles, and cardiac muscle. The CARDIAC muscle is unique because:

options.option_text: It is voluntary like skeletal muscle in adults
It is striated yet involuntary, only found in the heart
It is found in the walls of all hollow organs
It cannot contract without external nerve stimulus

questions.explanation: Cardiac muscle — striated (banded, like skeletal) but INVOLUNTARY (not under conscious control). Self-contracting (the heart's SA node generates its own rhythm — the heart can beat outside the body if blood-supplied). Found ONLY in the heart. Skeletal — striated + voluntary. Smooth — non-striated + involuntary, found in walls of hollow organs (intestines, blood vessels, uterus, bladder). Distractor 1 — cardiac is involuntary, not voluntary. Distractor 3 describes smooth muscle. Distractor 4 — wrong; cardiac contracts on its own.

questions.stem: The number of vertebrae in the human VERTEBRAL COLUMN (excluding the fused sacrum and coccyx) is:

options.option_text: 30 individual vertebrae stacked one on another
24 movable vertebrae in three regional groups
33 individual vertebrae from skull to tailbone
12 vertebrae running along the entire spine

questions.explanation: Movable vertebrae: 7 cervical (neck) + 12 thoracic (with ribs) + 5 lumbar (lower back) = 24. Plus FUSED: sacrum (5 vertebrae fused in adults) + coccyx (4 fused) = 33 total bones counting fused. Distractor 1 = 30 misses two fused groups partially. Distractor 3 = 33 includes fused sacrum/coccyx (both interpretations are valid; the question specified excluding fusions, so 24 is the correct strict answer). Distractor 4 = thoracic count alone.

questions.stem: Tendons are tough fibrous bands that connect:

options.option_text: Bone to bone across a joint to keep the joint stable
Muscle to bone, transmitting muscle force to the skeleton
Skin to underlying muscle, holding the skin in place
Nerve fibres to muscle endplates at the junction

questions.explanation: TENDONS — connect muscle to bone (e.g., Achilles tendon — calf muscle to heel bone; common cause of sports injury when ruptured). LIGAMENTS — connect bone to bone, stabilising joints (e.g., ACL in knee). FASCIA — sheets of tissue holding muscle groups together. The neuromuscular junction is a synaptic connection, not a tendon. Tendons are made primarily of type-I collagen, very strong in tension but inelastic.

questions.stem: Calcium and phosphorus together account for most of the mineral mass of bones. The crystalline mineral that gives bone its rigidity is called:

options.option_text: Calcium chloride, common as table-salt component
Hydroxyapatite, a calcium phosphate mineral lattice
Calcium carbonate, the main component of marble rock
Calcium sulphate, the principal substance in gypsum

questions.explanation: Hydroxyapatite — Ca₁₀(PO₄)₆(OH)₂. Forms ~70% of bone mass (giving rigidity); the rest is COLLAGEN (mostly type I, giving tensile strength). The combination is like reinforced concrete — crystals provide compression strength, collagen provides tension strength. Vitamin D regulates calcium absorption from gut → bone mineralisation. Distractor 1 = NaCl + minor Ca compounds, irrelevant. Distractor 3 = limestone / marble, mostly CaCO₃ but not bone. Distractor 4 = gypsum, used in plaster casts (irony: used externally to set fractures, but not the bone itself).
